provenance.note: Figures were gathered with WebSearch because WebFetch was blocked in the authoring session; every entry keeps the source URLs it was read from. This is a curated snapshot of public sources, not an authoritative database, and it is baked into the build — the app never fetches anything at runtime.
rules: A null field means the figure is not known or sources disagree irreconcilably. Omit the row — never substitute 0, "unknown", or a guess.
maxLenM is not always a length: read `measure`/`measureLabel` and label it with those words.
group:true entries name a group, not a species; show `groupLine` so the referent is explicit.
habitat freshwater/diadromous entries must say so rather than implying a marine depth.
Band figures (minM/maxM/preferM) are placement heuristics derived from the sourced ranges — they are not themselves sourced figures and must not be displayed as data.
The dot-creature is a procedural rendering, never a depiction of the real animal.

shoreZone is the CROSS-SHELF position the sources place the animal at, from the fixed set intertidal / nearshore / shelf / shelfbreak / slope / oceanic / abyssal. It is a habitat statement, not a coordinate.
benthic:true means the animal lives ON or IN the bottom. Placement puts it on the seabed at its own transect position, not in open water.
bioluminescent:false is a researched FALSE, not a missing value — a barreleye watches other animals' light and makes none of its own.

steps: band = the sourced "usually" range when one is quoted (usualMinM/usualMaxM), otherwise the shallow third of the sourced range, because published maxima are records rather than homes.
a band capped by an explicit caveat in the entry (bandCapM) is capped there, with the quote in bandCapNote.
preferM = sqrt(max(minM, maxM/20) * maxM) — the shallow-weighted centre of the band. Depth distributions are heavy at the shallow end.
a band narrower than min(max(0.6*preferM, 4), 60) m is widened up to that, never past the sourced extent, so a school still spreads.
maxima are clamped to 1190 m so nothing is placed inside the seabed.
motion (tight/hold/wander/note) is carried over from the v3.4 authored band; wanderM is rescaled to 12% of the new span.

v37.note: v3.7 species (datasets D-G) have no quoted "usually" range, so the band is the shallow third of the sourced range; a null depthMaxM borrows the depth envelope of the species' own shoreZone list (the record's null is untouched). preferM, widening and the 1190 m clamp are the v3.5 steps unchanged.

habitats.diadromous: diadromous — moves between fresh water and the sea

whale.fact: Its heart weighs ~180 kg and its calls reach 188 decibels.
whale.precision: Surface-breather; depth is dive range, not habitat. Foraging dives average ~140 m; deepest tagged dive ~316 m (Croll et al. 2001). Popular sources claiming 500 m are unsupported by tag data. Max length disputed: NOAA states 'about 110 ft' (~33.5 m) but the longest reliably measured specimen is 29.9 m, so 30 m is the defensible figure.

humpback.usualNote: 88.5% of 7,986 tagged dives were shallower than 80 m
humpback.fact: Males sing 20-minute songs, and every male in a region sings the same one.
humpback.precision: Surface-breather. In a South Pacific tagging study of 7,986 dives, 88.5% were shallower than 80 m; deepest recorded dive 616 m. Max length: longest recorded 17.4 m (male) and 18.6 m (female); 18.5 m used as an honest round figure. IUCN downlisted to Least Concern in the Nov 2018 cetacean update (several subpopulations remain EN/CR).

orca.fact: One of the few mammals that goes through menopause; females can pass 90 years.
orca.precision: Surface-breather. Deepest recorded dive 480 m, from Eastern North Pacific offshore killer whales; most foraging is far shallower and depth use varies hugely between ecotypes (resident/transient/offshore). Max length ~10 m for males, ~8.5 m for females. IUCN is Data Deficient specifically because the unresolved species/ecotype split blocks a global assessment.

beluga.fact: A tagged male dived to 956 m in the Canada Basin, under Arctic winter ice.
beluga.precision: Surface-breather. Maximum depth disputed and strongly population-dependent: 350 m in an early free-ranging study, 647 m (SeaWorld), 872 m often cited, and 956 m for a male in the Canada Basin (2016 study). 950 m used as a rounded upper bound; typical dives are far shallower. Deepest-diving stocks are Cumberland Sound, Somerset Island and West Greenland animals wintering over steep basins.

dolphin.usualNote: coastal populations typically dive only 3–46 m
dolphin.fact: Offshore ones dive to 1,000 m; coastal ones rarely go past 50 m.
dolphin.precision: Surface-breather. Depth range varies enormously by ecotype — this is the clearest case in the set. Coastal populations typically dive only 3-46 m; offshore Bermuda animals tagged by Fahlman et al. (2023) reached 1,000 m and 13.8 min. The old 300 m figure is from 'Tuffy', a US Navy-trained dolphin (1965), and badly understates wild capability.

narwhal.fact: Its 3 m tusk is a tooth wired with about 10 million nerve endings.
narwhal.precision: Surface-breather. Tag data show regular dives to 800-1,200 m with maxima exceeding 1,800 m. Max length is body length excluding the tusk (3.6-6.2 m; males average ~4.7 m). IUCN was Near Threatened 2008-2017, downlisted to Least Concern in the 2017 cetacean update — older sources still say NT.

porpoise.fact: Greenland porpoises dive past 400 m, far deeper than their North Sea kin.
porpoise.precision: Surface-breather. Depth varies strongly by population: North Sea animals max around 226 m, while West Greenland porpoises averaged 248 m maximum dive depth with a deepest of 410 m. Global IUCN is Least Concern, but the Baltic Proper and Black Sea subpopulations are separately assessed as far more threatened.

shark.fact: A tagged female named Nicole swam 11,100 km to Australia in 99 days.
shark.precision: FishBase gives depth 0-1280 m, usually 0-250 m; the deep end comes from tagged offshore excursions, not routine habitat. Max length 640 cm TL per FishBase; larger claims (7 m+) are historically unverified.

tuna.fact: Warm-blooded: it holds its core up to 20 C above the surrounding water.
tuna.precision: FishBase depth 0-985 m, usually 0-100 m. Max length 458 cm TL. IUCN moved this species from Endangered to Least Concern in the September 2021 Red List update after quota enforcement worked — many secondary sources (including FishBase text) still say Endangered.

marlin.fact: Adult females can outweigh the biggest males by roughly four times.
marlin.precision: FishBase depth range 0-1000 m for M. nigricans; no 'usually' band is published for this species (the 0-200 m figure often quoted belongs to the Indo-Pacific M. mazara). Max length 500 cm TL. Heaviest recorded female 748 kg vs 170 kg for the largest male. IUCN Vulnerable under criterion A2 (33-37% decline over 27 years).

swordfish.fact: Heater cells warm its eyes and brain 10-15 C above the surrounding sea.
swordfish.precision: FishBase depth 0-2878 m, usually 0-550 m; it makes large daily vertical migrations, which is what the heater organ protects against. Max length 455 cm FL (fork length, not total). Global IUCN assessment is old (2007/2011-era) and Near Threatened.

barracuda.fact: Large ones often carry ciguatoxin, which cooking cannot destroy.
barracuda.precision: FishBase depth 0-100 m, usually 3-30 m — much shallower than its reputation suggests. Max length 200 cm, max weight 50 kg. Widely quoted burst-speed figures (27-36 mph) conflict badly across sources and are deliberately excluded here.

sturgeon.fact: The oldest one recorded was 118 years old; a record fish weighed 1,571 kg.
sturgeon.precision: Beluga sturgeon used as the referent (largest sturgeon). FishBase depth 70-180 m in the sea, wintering to about 100 m; it is anadromous and runs far up rivers to spawn, so the marine band understates where it actually goes. Max length 800 cm TL per FishBase; largest well-documented specimen 720 cm / 1,571 kg.

sunfish.fact: The 2,744 kg heaviest-bony-fish record belongs to its cousin Mola alexandrini.
sunfish.precision: FishBase depth 30-1515 m, usually 30-70 m; it basks at the surface between deep foraging dives, so the shallow minimum of 30 m is a FishBase convention rather than a hard floor. Max length 333 cm TL, max published weight ~1.3 t. The famous 2,300 kg Kamogawa specimen was reidentified in 2022 as M. alexandrini, not M. mola.

oarfish.fact: Submersible footage shows it swimming vertically, head pointed at the surface.
oarfish.precision: FishBase depth 20-1000 m, usually 20-200 m. Max length: reliable records to 8 m; the widely repeated 11 m / 272 kg figure is a historical report and not verified, so 8 m is used. IUCN set to null — no global Red List assessment found for this species.

seahorse.fact: Males get pregnant, feeding embryos through a placenta-like brood pouch.
seahorse.precision: Spotted/common seahorse used as the referent for the generic lexicon word. FishBase depth 0-68 m, usually 0-8 m. Max length 30 cm TL. IUCN Vulnerable, assessed 2012.

moray.fact: A second set of jaws launches from its throat to drag prey down.
moray.precision: Giant moray used as the referent (largest Indo-Pacific moray). FishBase depth 0-50 m, max length 300 cm TL. The pharyngeal-jaw mechanism is from Mehta & Wainwright, Nature 449:79-82 (2007) and is a moray-family trait, not unique to this species.

lamprey.fact: One lamprey can kill up to 18 kg of fish during its parasitic phase.
lamprey.precision: FishBase gives an extraordinary depth range of 1-4099 m; the deep records come from lampreys attached to deep-caught host fish rather than free-living lampreys, so treat the maximum as host-mediated. Max length ~120 cm. Anadromous: spawns in fresh water, feeds at sea.
lamprey.bandCapNote: the deep records come from lampreys attached to deep-caught host fish rather than free-living lampreys

clownfish.fact: All are born male; the biggest fish in the anemone turns female when the queen dies.
clownfish.precision: FishBase: depth 1-15 m (usually 3-15 m), max 11.0 cm TL.

angelfish.measureNote: standard length — total length is slightly greater
angelfish.fact: Juveniles wear blue-white bullseye rings; scientists once called them a separate species.
angelfish.precision: FishBase: 1-100 m, max 40.0 cm SL (standard length, so total length is slightly greater).

lionfish.fact: In the invaded Caribbean, one female can release over 2 million eggs a year.
lionfish.precision: FishBase native-range depth 2-55 m; in the invaded W Atlantic recorded to 304 m off Bermuda. Max 38 cm (43 cm reported in invaded range).

pufferfish.fact: Its tetrodotoxin is roughly 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide, with no antidote.
pufferfish.precision: "Pufferfish" is a family-level name; figures here are for the white-spotted puffer Arothron hispidus (FishBase: 1-50 m, 50 cm TL).

anglerfish.fact: Males are 2-3 cm, fuse to the female's body, and share her bloodstream for life.
anglerfish.precision: Depth 100-4500 m, usually 100-1500 m. Max length is the female (18.0 cm TL); males reach only 1.5-2.8 cm.

salmon.fact: The longest ever netted, in Norway in 1925, measured 160.65 cm.
salmon.precision: FishBase: 0-210 m (usually 10-23 m), max 150 cm; the 160.65 cm Norwegian record is the longest documented individual. Anadromous - spawns in fresh water, matures at sea.

cod.fact: A single large female can release up to 9 million eggs in one spawning.
cod.precision: FishBase: 0-600 m, usually 150-200 m; record 200 cm TL / ~96 kg.

herring.fact: They talk by farting: high-pitched anal gas pulses predators can't hear.
herring.precision: FishBase: 0-364 m, usually 0-200 m; max 45 cm.

mackerel.fact: No swim bladder at all, so it must keep swimming or sink.
mackerel.precision: FishBase: 0-1000 m, usually 0-200 m; max 60.0 cm FL (fork length).

sardine.groupNote: 'Sardine' covers several clupeid genera (Sardinops, Sardina, Sardinella); figures here are Sardinops sagax
sardine.groupTaxon: 'Sardine' covers several clupeid genera (Sardinops, Sardina, Sardinella); figures here are Sardinops sagax
sardine.fact: The South African sardine run forms shoals kilometres long and tens of metres deep.
sardine.precision: 39.5 cm SL. IUCN null - Sardinops sagax is not evaluated on the Red List. Reported sardine-run shoal dimensions vary widely between sources (roughly 7-15 km long, 1.5-4 km wide, 30-40 m deep), so the fact avoids a single number. 'Sardine' also covers Sardina pilchardus and other clupeids. — Referent detail (Sardina pilchardus, species-B): FishBase 10-100 m (usually 25-100 m), max 27.5 cm SL.
sardine.locationNote: cool coastal shelf seas, in dense shoals near the surface

piranha.fact: Shoaling is defence, not frenzy: lone piranhas breathe faster from fear.
piranha.precision: Depth nulled - FishBase lists no depth range for this Amazon-basin freshwater species and no sourced figure was found. Max 50 cm SL (rarely over 35 cm). No IUCN global assessment located.

grouper.fact: Booms at about 60 Hz with its swim bladder; divers feel the thump.
grouper.precision: FishBase: 0-100 m, usually 0-46 m; max 250 cm (dominant males), ~400 kg. IUCN VU (A2bcd, 2021 assessment).

snapper.fact: Otolith dating has confirmed individuals up to 57-60 years old.
snapper.precision: FishBase: 10-190 m, usually 30-130 m; max 100 cm TL. IUCN VU A2bd (2015 assessment).

trout.fact: Steelhead are the same species: rainbow trout that went to sea.
trout.precision: Flagged freshwater per brief, but O. mykiss also has an anadromous sea-run form (steelhead); FishBase lists it as freshwater/brackish/marine. Depth 0-200 m, max 122 cm TL (sea-run individuals).

bass.fact: Slow-grower: up to 30 years old, and 7 years just to reach legal size.
bass.precision: FishBase: 10-100 m, max 103 cm TL. IUCN category disputed across sources - Near Threatened per FishBase and a 2024 global reassessment, Least Concern in older assessments.

catfish.fact: Some beach themselves to snatch pigeons, succeeding about 28% of the time.
catfish.precision: Max length disputed: 2.73 m / 130 kg is the largest with hard evidence; the widely repeated 5 m / 306 kg figures trace to misidentifications and unit errors. Depth 0-30 m; occasionally enters brackish Baltic/Black Sea water.

wrasse.fact: It scraped a mark it could only see in a mirror - a first for fish.
wrasse.precision: FishBase: 0-100 m, usually 1-30 m; max 14.0 cm TL. The mirror-mark result is real but its interpretation as self-awareness is contested.

koi.fact: Koi are colour morphs of the Amur carp, bred ornamentally since the 1820s.
koi.precision: Both depth and max length nulled. No depth range published for this species. Length figures conflict badly and irreconcilably: FishBase gives 28.0 cm SL for wild Amur carp, while ~90-100 cm is widely claimed for ornamental koi but only in non-scientific hobbyist sources.

goldfish.fact: The 3-second memory is a myth; trained goldfish recall tasks months later.
goldfish.precision: FishBase: 0-20 m, max 48.0 cm TL (occasional reports to 59 cm). Freshwater/brackish. IUCN LC, assessed 2010.

minnow.fact: Its crushed skin releases 'Schreckstoff', the alarm pheromone found in 1938.
minnow.precision: Depth nulled - no published depth range found for this small stream species. Max 14 cm TL (typically ~7 cm). IUCN LC, assessed January 2024.

guppy.fact: Under new predators, wild guppies evolve measurably in as few as 8 generations.
guppy.precision: Depth nulled - FishBase publishes no depth range. Max length is the female (~5 cm); males ~3.5 cm. IUCN category not confirmed by any source consulted.

betta.fact: A labyrinth organ lets it gulp air; fry ride in the male's bubble nest.
betta.precision: Depth nulled - no published range; wild habitat is shallow rice paddies and stagnant pools. Max 6.5 cm TL. IUCN VU in the wild (habitat loss and pollution), despite being ubiquitous in the aquarium trade.

tetra.fact: Its blue stripe is tilting guanine crystals - it dims to indigo in the dark.
tetra.precision: Depth nulled - no published range; native to blackwater tributaries of the Solimoes. Length is FishBase's 2.5 cm SL; ~4 cm TL is commonly reported elsewhere. No IUCN assessment located.

perch.fact: Lays eggs in white lace ribbons up to a metre long, unique to Perca.
perch.precision: FishBase: 1-30 m, usually 3-4 m; max 60.0 cm SL; maximum recorded age 22 years.

pike.fact: Strikes from a standstill at up to 130 m/s2 acceleration.
pike.precision: FishBase: 0-30 m, usually 1-5 m; max 150 cm TL (female), 137 cm FL (male). IUCN LC, assessed 2022. Acceleration measured on ~0.38 m fish.

carp.fact: IUCN Vulnerable in its native range while ranking among the worst invaders.
carp.precision: FishBase: 0-29 m, max 110 cm SL. Freshwater/brackish, benthopelagic.

manta.fact: Highest brain-to-body ratio of any fish; may pass mirror self-recognition.
manta.precision: Size is DISC WIDTH, not body length: 700 cm max (7.1 m measured in one case). Depth 0-1000 m. Uplisted to Endangered in December 2020; some sources still cite the older Vulnerable listing.

stingray.fact: The serrated venomous barb regrows like a fingernail in 3-4 months.
stingray.precision: Size is DISC WIDTH: FishBase 200 cm WD, though 150 cm WD is cited elsewhere. FishBase depth 0-53 m; other sources report the species to 100 m.

skate.fact: At 2.85 m it's the largest skate in European seas - and Critically Endangered.
skate.precision: "Common skate" was split into two species (D. batis and D. intermedius); the 285 cm figure was recorded for the historical D. batis complex, so it may partly reflect flapper skate.

flounder.fact: Born with an eye on each side; one migrates over the skull as it flattens.
flounder.precision: FishBase: 1-100 m, max 60.0 cm TL. Regularly enters estuaries and fresh water.

halibut.fact: World's largest flatfish: 4.7 m, 320 kg, and up to 50 years old.
halibut.precision: IUCN nulled - sources give three different categories (Endangered from the outdated 1996 assessment, Near Threatened, and Vulnerable), so no category is well-established. Depth 50-2000 m, max 470 cm TL.

sole.fact: Lies buried in sand by day with only eyes and nostrils showing.
sole.precision: FishBase: 0-150 m, usually 10-60 m; max 70.0 cm SL. IUCN Data Deficient.

eel.fact: Swims ~5,000 km to the Sargasso Sea; its eyes swell up to 10x first.
eel.precision: FishBase: 0-700 m; max 150 cm (exceptional - normally 60-80 cm). Catadromous: grows in fresh water, spawns in the Atlantic. IUCN CR, assessed 2018.

seasnake.groupNote: True sea snakes, subfamily Hydrophiinae of the Elapidae, roughly 60-70 fully marine species; the widespread pelagic example is Hydrophis platurus, the yellow-bellied sea snake.
seasnake.groupTaxon: True sea snakes, subfamily Hydrophiinae of the Elapidae, roughly 60-70 fully marine species; the widespread pelagic example is Hydrophis platurus, the yellow-bellied sea snake.
seasnake.groupReferent: Hydrophis platurus, the yellow-bellied sea snake
seasnake.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: most species stay above about 100 m
seasnake.fact: Some take up to a third of their oxygen straight through their skin.
seasnake.precision: GROUP figures, not one species, and iucn is null because statuses differ by species. Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Most species stay above about 100 m; foraging at roughly 250 m was published in 2019 as the first mesopelagic records for the group. Length: most adults 1-1.5 m, maximum about 2.7 m in the largest Hydrophis. Species count is 60-70 depending on authority (one source says 54 in 16 genera). Cutaneous oxygen uptake is reported variously as 20-33%, so 'up to a third' is the honest phrasing. — Referent detail (Hydrophis platurus, species-B): Approximate. This is a surface-pelagic snake; the depth figure is measured maximum dive depth (6.8 m dry season, 15.1 m wet season), not a habitat range. Max length ~1.2 m; adults commonly 50-90 cm.
seasnake.locationNote: warm coastal waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans over reefs, mangroves and soft bottoms; the yellow-bellied sea snake drifts in the open ocean far from land

pipefish.fact: The male gets pregnant, brooding eggs in a pouch of two skin folds.
pipefish.precision: FishBase: 0-110 m, usually 3-15 m; max 50.0 cm TL. IUCN LC per Wikipedia; one aggregator lists no assessment.

ribbonfish.fact: A 3 m ribbon that swims vertically, head up, in 300-600 m of water.
ribbonfish.precision: FishBase: bathypelagic, 300-600 m, max 300 cm TL. Looks like an oarfish but is not closely related.

jellyfish.usualNote: other sources give 0–90 m because the animal is almost always near the surface
jellyfish.fact: Moon jellies drift near the surface but have been recorded down to about 1,250 m.
jellyfish.precision: maxLenM is bell diameter: usually ~25 cm, commonly cited max 40 cm (some sources say 50 cm). SeaLifeBase gives depth 0-1250 m; other sources give 0-90 m because the animal is almost always near the surface. IUCN: not evaluated (NE).

manowar.measureNote: disputed: commonly 10–20 m extended; the float itself is ~0.3 m
manowar.fact: Not a jellyfish but a floating colony of four kinds of specialised zooids.
manowar.precision: Obligate surface floater, so depth is 0 m; the float itself is ~0.3 m and rises ~15 cm above the waterline. maxLenM is tentacle length, which is disputed: commonly 10-20 m extended, reported to 30 m and claimed to 50 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

seaangel.measureNote: northern subspecies; the southern one is only ~1.2 cm
seaangel.fact: A shell-less swimming sea slug; the northern form reaches 8.5 cm, largest of any sea angel.
seaangel.precision: Northern subspecies 7-8.5 cm; southern subspecies only ~1.2 cm. Depth given variously as surface to >500 m and 0-600 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

comb.commonName: comb jelly (warty comb jelly / sea walnut)
comb.groupNote: "Comb jelly" is the whole phylum Ctenophora (~200 described species). Referent chosen: Mnemiopsis leidyi.
comb.groupTaxon: "Comb jelly" is the whole phylum Ctenophora (~200 described species).
comb.groupReferent: the warty comb jelly / sea walnut, Mnemiopsis leidyi
comb.fact: Its eight comb rows of fused cilia scatter light into rainbows - diffraction, not bioluminescence.
comb.precision: SeaLifeBase max length 18 cm; other sources give 7-12 cm as typical. Depth 5-200 m (pelagic) per SeaLifeBase. Ctenophores are the largest animals that swim using cilia. IUCN: not evaluated. — v3.7: species-G researched the PHYLUM Ctenophora separately (~200 species, 0-7,000 m, maxLenM 1.5 m for the ribbon-shaped Cestum veneris while most comb jellies are 1-10 cm); those group-wide figures are NOT the ones above, which are Mnemiopsis leidyi’s. From that record: most species luminesce but some groups appear incapable of it; the famous shimmering rainbow is diffraction off beating cilia, a separate phenomenon from the bioluminescence; benthic is false for the great majority, but creeping platyctenids do live on the bottom; not assessed by IUCN.
comb.bioNote: blue-green flashes from the canals under the comb rows when disturbed

octopus.fact: Reaches about 1.3 m in total length with a mantle of roughly 25 cm.
octopus.precision: maxLenM is total length (arms included): males to 1.3 m, females to 1.2 m. Mantle length ~0.25 m. Depth 0-200 m.

squid.measureNote: to the tentacle tips; mantle alone ~2 m
squid.fact: Has the largest eyes of any invertebrate and is known mostly from strandings and whale stomachs.
squid.precision: Depth range is poorly known; 300-1,000 m is inferred from trawls and sperm whale dive behaviour. Max total length 12-13 m for females, ~10 m for males, measured to the tentacle tips; claims of 20 m+ are undocumented. Mantle alone ~2 m.

kraken.commonName: kraken (legend; represented by the giant squid)
kraken.groupNote: The kraken is a Scandinavian legendary sea monster, not a taxon. Referent used, per instruction: Architeuthis dux (giant squid).
kraken.groupTaxon: The kraken is a Scandinavian legendary sea monster, not a taxon.
kraken.measureNote: to the tentacle tips; mantle alone ~2 m
kraken.fact: The kraken legend is usually traced to real giant squid, which reach about 13 m.
kraken.precision: All figures are for Architeuthis dux and carry the same caveats as the 'squid' entry. No figure here describes the mythological kraken itself.

cuttlefish.fact: Moves inshore to spawn in spring and summer, wintering at 100-200 m.
cuttlefish.precision: maxLenM is mantle length (49 cm typical maximum; largest recorded individual 60 cm ML). SeaLifeBase depth 0-242 m, usually 0-50 m.

nautilus.fact: Lives on steep reef drop-offs and implodes below roughly 800 m.
nautilus.precision: maxLenM is shell diameter: typically 170-180 mm, up to 222 mm. Depth typically 130-700 m; shell implosion depth commonly quoted as ~2,000 ft (~610 m) to ~800 m, so the deep limit is disputed. IUCN: no nautilus species is currently assessed on the Red List; listed as Threatened under the US ESA (2018) and on CITES Appendix II (2017).

vampyroteuthis.usualNote: typical band 600–1200 m; MBARI found it confined to 600–900 m in Monterey Bay
vampyroteuthis.fact: Lives in the oxygen minimum zone, where oxygen falls to about 0.4 ml per litre.
vampyroteuthis.precision: Meso- to bathypelagic 300-3,000 m; typical band 600-1,200 m, and MBARI work in Monterey Bay found it confined to 600-900 m. Max total length reported as 28-30 cm; mantle length usually 7.9-12.1 cm. IUCN: not evaluated. — v3.7: Mantle length is ~13-15 cm; the 30 cm figure is total length including arms. Depth records span 300-3000 m; MBARI finds it concentrated near 600-900 m in the Monterey Bay oxygen minimum zone. Not assessed by IUCN.
vampyroteuthis.locationNote: open-ocean midwater, in the low-oxygen layer of tropical and temperate seas worldwide
vampyroteuthis.bioNote: photophores on fins and arm tips flash blue; ejects glowing mucus instead of ink

starfish.groupNote: "Starfish" is the class Asteroidea (~1,900 species). Referent chosen: Asterias rubens, the common sea star of the North Atlantic.
starfish.groupReferent: Asterias rubens, the common sea star of the North Atlantic
starfish.measureNote: arm tip to arm tip; 10–30 cm is normal
starfish.fact: Ranges from the intertidal down to about 650 m and can span 52 cm across.
starfish.precision: maxLenM is arm-tip-to-arm-tip diameter; 52 cm is the recorded maximum, 10-30 cm is normal. Depth 0-650 m, usually 0-400 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

urchin.groupNote: "Sea urchin" is the class Echinoidea (~950 species). Referent chosen: Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the purple sea urchin of the NE Pacific.
urchin.groupTaxon: "Sea urchin" is the class Echinoidea (~950 species).
urchin.groupReferent: Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the purple sea urchin of the NE Pacific
urchin.measureNote: usually ~50 mm; spines add to overall size
urchin.fact: Grinds pits into rock with its teeth and spines and can strip kelp forests bare.
urchin.precision: maxLenM is test (shell) diameter: usually ~50 mm, occasionally 100 mm; spines add to overall size. Depth mid-to-low intertidal down to 160 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

crab.groupNote: "Crab" is the infraorder Brachyura plus other decapods (~7,000 species). Referent chosen: Callinectes sapidus, the Atlantic blue crab.
crab.groupTaxon: "Crab" is the infraorder Brachyura plus other decapods (~7,000 species).
crab.groupReferent: Callinectes sapidus, the Atlantic blue crab
crab.measureNote: carapace length is roughly half that
crab.fact: An estuarine swimming crab found from the shoreline down to about 90 m.
crab.precision: maxLenM is carapace WIDTH (up to 23 cm), the standard measurement for this species; carapace length is roughly half that. Depth 0-90 m, usually 0-35 m. IUCN status not confirmed in any source found, so left null.

sanddollar.groupNote: "Sand dollar" is the order Clypeasteroida. Referent chosen: Echinarachnius parma, the common sand dollar of the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
sanddollar.groupReferent: Echinarachnius parma, the common sand dollar of the North Atlantic and North Pacific
sanddollar.fact: A flattened burrowing urchin recorded from the low tide line down to about 1,500 m.
sanddollar.precision: maxLenM is test diameter, 5-10 cm when fully grown. The 1,500 m (5,000 ft) figure is an occasional extreme; the species is normally shallow subtidal. IUCN: not evaluated.
sanddollar.bandCapNote: the 1,500 m figure is an occasional extreme; the species is normally shallow subtidal

basketstar.groupNote: "Basket star" is the family Gorgonocephalidae. Referent chosen: Gorgonocephalus arcticus, the northern basket star.
basketstar.groupReferent: Gorgonocephalus arcticus, the northern basket star
basketstar.measureNote: other Gorgonocephalus species unfurl to ~1.2 m
basketstar.fact: A brittle star whose arms branch repeatedly into a filter-feeding basket.
basketstar.precision: maxLenM is total diameter, up to ~400 mm for this species; other Gorgonocephalus species unfurl to ~1.2 m. Depth low intertidal / sublittoral down to 1,500 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

brittlestar.groupNote: "Brittle star" is the class Ophiuroidea (~2,000+ species). Referent chosen: Ophiothrix fragilis, the common brittle star of NE Atlantic waters.
brittlestar.groupTaxon: "Brittle star" is the class Ophiuroidea (~2,000+ species).
brittlestar.groupReferent: Ophiothrix fragilis, the common brittle star of NE Atlantic waters
brittlestar.measureNote: one arm; full span is roughly 20 cm
brittlestar.fact: Forms dense beds where thousands of arms sieve food from the current.
brittlestar.precision: maxLenM is single arm length (~10 cm); the central disc is up to 2 cm across and arms are about five times the disc diameter, so full span is roughly 20 cm. Depth: shallow to 350 m (some sources say 200 m). IUCN: not evaluated.

anemone.groupNote: "Sea anemone" is the order Actiniaria (~1,100 species). Referent chosen: Actinia equina, the beadlet anemone.
anemone.groupTaxon: "Sea anemone" is the order Actiniaria (~1,100 species).
anemone.fact: Survives hours of air exposure at low tide by pulling its tentacles into a jelly blob.
anemone.precision: maxLenM is diameter when expanded (under 10 cm); height 6-8 cm, basal disc up to 5 cm. Mainly intertidal, rarely subtidal to ~20 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

coral.groupNote: "Reef-building coral" spans hundreds of scleractinian species. Referent chosen: Acropora cervicornis, Caribbean staghorn coral.
coral.groupTaxon: "Reef-building coral" spans hundreds of scleractinian species.
coral.usualNote: the typical depth band on forereefs is 5–25 m
coral.fact: One of the fastest-growing corals, adding up to about 20 cm of branch a year.
coral.precision: maxLenM is branch length (a few cm to over 2 m). Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2008; population declined at least 80% over 30 years and is now under 3% of former abundance. Typical depth band on forereefs is 5-25 m.

kelp.usualNote: anchors on rock mostly at 6–30 m and needs bottom light above 1% of surface
kelp.measureNote: holdfast to canopy; reports up to 60 m
kelp.fact: Among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth, adding up to 50 cm a day.
kelp.precision: maxLenM is frond height from holdfast to canopy: commonly 30-45 m, with reports up to 60 m. Anchors on rock mostly at 6-30 m and needs bottom light above 1% of surface, so it rarely exceeds ~40 m. IUCN: no Red List assessment found.

seagrass.groupNote: "Seagrass" covers ~72 species of marine flowering plants. Referent chosen: Thalassia testudinum, Caribbean turtlegrass.
seagrass.groupTaxon: "Seagrass" covers ~72 species of marine flowering plants.
seagrass.usualNote: to 30 m where water is clear, typically 0–10 m
seagrass.fact: A true flowering plant, not an alga, forming meadows down to about 30 m in clear water.
seagrass.precision: maxLenM is blade length, reported as up to 30 cm in some sources and 10-60 cm in others. Depth to 30 m where water is clear, typically 0-10 m. IUCN Least Concern (2010 global assessment); a 2025 Tropical Atlantic regional assessment raised it to Near Threatened, so the status is in flux.

seaweed.groupNote: "Seaweed" is an informal term for thousands of marine macroalgae. Referent chosen: Fucus vesiculosus, bladderwrack.
seaweed.groupTaxon: "Seaweed" is an informal term for thousands of marine macroalgae.
seaweed.fact: Paired gas bladders lift its fronds toward the light as the tide comes in.
seaweed.precision: depthMaxM is null on purpose: MarLIN states depth is not a meaningful variable because the species is intertidal, occurring only at shallow depths in the low-salinity Baltic. Length usually 20-60 cm, growing to 150 cm and recorded to 2 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

sargassum.groupNote: Sargassum is a genus of ~350 species; the floating Atlantic mats are mainly S. natans and S. fluitans. Referent chosen: Sargassum natans.
sargassum.groupTaxon: Sargassum is a genus of ~350 species; the floating Atlantic mats are mainly S. natans and S. fluitans.
sargassum.fact: In June 2018 the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt ran 8,850 km and held over 20 million tonnes.
sargassum.precision: Holopelagic: it never attaches to the seafloor and lives at the surface, hence depth 0 m. maxLenM is frond length (roughly 10-200 cm); mats themselves stretch far further. IUCN: not evaluated.
sargassum.surfaceFloater: holopelagic — it never attaches to the seafloor

wakame.fact: One of the world's most invasive seaweeds, now on every continent except Africa and Antarctica.
wakame.precision: Fronds usually reach 1.5 m and have been recorded to 3 m; growth up to 1 cm/day. Depth low intertidal to 18 m (some sources say 15-20 m), with most biomass at 1-3 m. IUCN: not Red List assessed, but listed in the IUCN Global Invasive Species Database.

eelgrass.usualNote: MarLIN: typically down to 4 m in sheltered UK waters
eelgrass.fact: Meadows of it store carbon and shelter juvenile fish in sheltered bays and estuaries.
eelgrass.precision: Depth is light-limited and highly site-specific: MarLIN gives 'typically down to 4 m' in sheltered UK waters, and a Kiel Bight (Baltic) study records 0.6-7.6 m, which is the figure used here. It is not a global maximum. Leaves usually 20-50 cm, up to 2 m.

seafan.groupNote: "Sea fan" / gorgonian covers hundreds of octocoral species. Referent chosen: Gorgonia ventalina, the Caribbean common sea fan.
seafan.groupTaxon: "Sea fan" / gorgonian covers hundreds of octocoral species.
seafan.groupReferent: Gorgonia ventalina, the Caribbean common sea fan
seafan.measureNote: colony height; up to 150 cm wide
seafan.fact: Grows as a flat mesh oriented across the prevailing current to strain out plankton.
seafan.precision: maxLenM is colony height, up to 180 cm tall and 150 cm wide. Depth roughly 1-30 m (3-100 ft); most common shallower than ~15 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

plankton.groupNote: "Phytoplankton" is a functional group of thousands of species (diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, cyanobacteria). Referent chosen: Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, formerly Emiliania huxleyi.
plankton.groupTaxon: "Phytoplankton" is a functional group of thousands of species (diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, cyanobacteria).
plankton.usualNote: the euphotic zone, ~0–200 m in clear water
plankton.fact: Its chalk-plated blooms cover over 100,000 square kilometres and are visible from space.
plankton.precision: maxLenM is cell diameter, about 5 micrometres = 5e-6 m. Phytoplankton span <1 to >100 micrometres. Depth is the euphotic zone, ~0-200 m in clear water. NOAA credits the ocean, chiefly phytoplankton, with roughly half of Earth's photosynthetic oxygen production. IUCN: not evaluated (no Red List assessments exist for phytoplankton).

krill.measureNote: disputed: BAS says up to 6 cm, SeaLifeBase records 3.0 cm
krill.fact: One of the most abundant animals on Earth, with biomass estimated near 379 million tonnes.
krill.precision: Length is disputed: the British Antarctic Survey states up to 6 cm, while SeaLifeBase records a maximum of 3.0 cm TL. Depth normally 0-300 m (usually 15-130 m) with adults occasionally to 600 m; BAS has filmed krill feeding down to 3,000 m, so 600 m is a conservative maximum. IUCN Least Concern, assessed 2015.

shrimp.groupNote: "Shrimp" spans thousands of caridean and penaeid species. Referent chosen: Pandalus borealis, the northern or coldwater shrimp.
shrimp.groupTaxon: "Shrimp" spans thousands of caridean and penaeid species.
shrimp.groupReferent: Pandalus borealis, the northern or coldwater shrimp
shrimp.fact: Starts life male and later changes sex to female, a pattern called protandry.
shrimp.precision: maxLenM is female maximum (16.5 cm); males reach 12.0 cm. Depth 9-1,450 m, usually 50-500 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

salp.groupNote: "Salp" is the family Salpidae (~50 species). Referent chosen: Salpa fusiformis, the common salp.
salp.fact: A barrel-shaped tunicate that links into drifting chains and migrates up each night to feed.
salp.precision: maxLenM 5.2 cm for a single zooid; solitary zooids are usually 22-52 mm. Depth 0-800 m with diel vertical migration. IUCN: not evaluated.

algae.groupNote: "Algae" is an informal grouping of many unrelated lineages. Referent chosen: Ulva lactuca, sea lettuce, a green macroalga.
algae.groupTaxon: "Algae" is an informal grouping of many unrelated lineages.
algae.groupReferent: Ulva lactuca, sea lettuce, a green macroalga
algae.fact: Its blade is only two cells thick, which is why it looks like translucent green paper.
algae.precision: SeaLifeBase gives max length 100 cm and depth 0-108 m; most individuals are far smaller (18-30 cm) and blades over 40 cm occur only in sheltered sites. IUCN: not evaluated.

seaotter.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: most foraging dives 2–30 m
seaotter.fact: Densest fur of any mammal; it carries no blubber at all.
seaotter.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range, not a habitat band. Most foraging dives 2-30 m; mean maximum foraging depth 61 m; deepest confirmed dive 97 m. Length 1.0-1.5 m INCLUDING tail, males largest. Dives to the bottom to forage but does not live there, so benthic=false.
seaotter.locationNote: kelp forests and rocky shallows within 1-2 km of cold North Pacific coasts

seal.groupNote: Lexicon word 'seal' names the true seals, family Phocidae (~19 species); all figures here are for the harbour seal, Phoca vitulina.
seal.groupTaxon: Lexicon word 'seal' names the true seals, family Phocidae (~19 species); all figures here are for the harbour seal, Phoca vitulina.
seal.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: a typical dive is about 91 m
seal.fact: Pups can dive for two minutes when only two or three days old.
seal.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Typical dive about 91 m; maxima near 500 m reported from high-Arctic tagging, so 500 is an extreme not a normal. Length 1.5-1.9 m. Intertidal zone is haul-out use, not feeding.
seal.locationNote: temperate and Arctic coasts of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, hauling out on tidal rocks, sandbars and ice

sealion.groupNote: Lexicon word 'sea lion' names the six living otariine species; all figures here are for the California sea lion, Zalophus californianus.
sealion.groupTaxon: Lexicon word 'sea lion' names the six living otariine species; all figures here are for the California sea lion, Zalophus californianus.
sealion.groupReferent: the California sea lion, Zalophus californianus
sealion.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: most dives under 80 m
sealion.fact: Rotates its hind flippers forward to walk on land; true seals cannot.
sealion.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Most dives under 80 m and under 3 minutes; deepest well-documented dive 274 m. A 536 m figure circulates in aggregator databases and is NOT supported by the diving-behaviour literature, so it was rejected. Males to 2.4 m, females about 2.0 m.
sealion.locationNote: rocky islands, breakwaters and coasts from British Columbia to Baja California, feeding over the inner shelf

walrus.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: most foraging dives 10–100 m
walrus.fact: Its tusks are canine teeth up to a metre long, used to haul out onto ice.
walrus.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Most foraging dives 10-100 m, matching bivalve prey; four tagged dives over 500 m are the deepest ever documented. Length: Pacific males reach about 3.6 m, Atlantic males average about 3 m, females smaller. Species assessed Vulnerable; the Pacific subspecies is Data Deficient. Feeds ON the bottom but does not live there, so benthic=false.
walrus.locationNote: Arctic continental shelves, ploughing shallow shelf mud for clams and resting on drifting sea ice or coastal haul-outs

emperorpenguin.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: the 564 m record is one bird in 1994; ordinary foraging dives are far shallower
emperorpenguin.fact: Holds the record for the deepest dive by any bird, at 564 m.
emperorpenguin.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. The 564 m record is a single bird from Auster colony in 1994 (Wienecke et al. 2007); ordinary foraging dives are far shallower. Height 1.1-1.3 m standing. IUCN uplisted from Near Threatened to ENDANGERED in April 2026 - older sources still say Near Threatened.
emperorpenguin.locationNote: Antarctic coastal fast ice; forages over the continental shelf and, when fast ice blocks the shelf, out over the shelf break and slope

littlepenguin.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: spends most time within 5 m of the surface
littlepenguin.fact: The smallest penguin; it only crosses the beach to its burrow after dark.
littlepenguin.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Spends most time within 5 m of the surface; 67 m is a recorded maximum. Height 30-33 cm standing. Taxonomy disputed: some authorities split Eudyptula into two species across the Tasman. Intertidal zone reflects the nightly beach crossing, not feeding.
littlepenguin.locationNote: southern Australian and New Zealand coasts, nesting in shore burrows and feeding in inshore water mostly within 5 m of the surface

seaturtle.groupNote: Lexicon word 'sea turtle' names all seven living species (Cheloniidae plus Dermochelyidae); all figures here are for the green turtle, Chelonia mydas.
seaturtle.groupTaxon: Lexicon word 'sea turtle' names all seven living species (Cheloniidae plus Dermochelyidae); all figures here are for the green turtle, Chelonia mydas.
seaturtle.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: most of the day is spent on dives shallower than 20 m
seaturtle.fact: Named for the green fat under its shell, coloured by its seagrass diet.
seaturtle.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Most of the day is spent on dives shallower than 20 m; 138 m is a recorded maximum. maxLenM is CARAPACE length (up to ~1.4 m), not total animal length. Globally Endangered; several regional subpopulations are assessed separately with different statuses. Oceanic zone applies to the juvenile drift phase; intertidal is nesting only.
seaturtle.locationNote: tropical and subtropical seagrass meadows and reefs; hatchlings drift in the open ocean for years before settling onto coastal feeding grounds

leatherback.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: routine dives are shallow; dives of 300–1,250 m are infrequent
leatherback.fact: Dives past 1,200 m, deeper than any other reptile.
leatherback.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Routine dives are shallow; extraordinary dives of 300-1,250 m are infrequent, with 1,280 m the quoted ceiling. maxLenM is CARAPACE length: usual curved carapace length 1.43-1.70 m, NOAA gives 'more than 2 m' as the upper size, so 2.0 is conservative. The famous 1988 Harlech specimen's 2.91 m is a TOTAL length measured over the carapace and its curved carapace length is now disputed (re-inspection suggests ~1.5 m). Species is Vulnerable but individual subpopulations range from Endangered to Critically Endangered. Intertidal is nesting only.
leatherback.locationNote: open ocean worldwide, from tropical nesting beaches to cold temperate feeding grounds, chasing jellyfish in the water column

hawksbill.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: up to 92% of the day is spent on 2–20 m dives
hawksbill.fact: Eats sponges; its overlapping shell plates were the source of tortoiseshell.
hawksbill.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE range. Up to 92% of the day is spent on 2-20 m dives; eastern Pacific adults forage at mesophotic 30-150 m with modal depths of 35-40 m, which is the basis for depthMaxM=150. A 200 m maximum is quoted by secondary sources but I could NOT confirm it in a primary source, so it was not used. maxLenM is CARAPACE length (85-110 cm). Intertidal is nesting only.
hawksbill.locationNote: tropical coral reefs and rocky bottoms; some eastern Pacific populations feed almost entirely on submerged banks at 30-150 m

dugong.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: usually within about 10 m
dugong.fact: The only strictly marine mammal that is entirely herbivorous.
dugong.precision: Air-breather: depth is a DIVE/occupancy range. Usually within about 10 m; feeding dives recorded to about 37-39 m on deeper seagrass. Length up to about 3 m. Grazes ON the bottom but does not live there, so benthic=false. Unlike manatees it never enters fresh water.
dugong.locationNote: shallow seagrass meadows in sheltered bays, mangrove channels and inter-reef waters across some 40 Indo-West Pacific countries

manatee.groupNote: Lexicon word 'manatee' names the three species of Trichechus; all figures here are for the West Indian manatee, Trichechus manatus.
manatee.groupTaxon: Lexicon word 'manatee' names the three species of Trichechus; all figures here are for the West Indian manatee, Trichechus manatus.
manatee.groupReferent: the West Indian manatee, Trichechus manatus
manatee.fact: Its molars march forward and drop out, replaced from the back, for life.
manatee.precision: depthMaxM is NULL: no reliable maximum dive depth was found in any authoritative source. Manatees are strictly shallow-water animals, generally in water only a few metres deep. Length averages about 3 m, with individuals to about 4.5 m including the tail. habitat is set 'marine' but the species is euryhaline rather than truly marine - it needs fresh water to drink and spends much of the year in rivers and springs; it is not diadromous in the migratory-breeding sense. It never reaches the outer shelf.
manatee.locationNote: warm shallow coasts, estuaries, canals and rivers of Florida, the Caribbean and northern South America, moving freely between salt and fresh water

marineiguana.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: typical foraging dives are only 1.5–5 m
marineiguana.fact: Shrinks up to 20% in body length to survive El Nino food shortages.
marineiguana.precision: Air-breather, and shore-tied: depth is a DIVE range. Typical foraging dives are only 1.5-5 m; large adults have been recorded to about 30 m. Length about 1.3 m for adult males including tail, about 0.6 m for females, so maxLenM is the male figure. Most individuals feed in the intertidal without diving at all - routine subtidal diving is largely a large-male behaviour. Endemic to the Galapagos, so the range is tiny.
marineiguana.locationNote: Galapagos lava shorelines only; basks on intertidal rock and grazes algae in the shallows just offshore

polarbear.usualNote: a dive range, not a habitat band: typical dives 3–4.5 m
polarbear.fact: Its longest recorded dive lasted 3 min 10 s, stalking bearded seals.
polarbear.precision: FLAG: marine-ASSOCIATED, not marine. It is legally and biologically classed as a marine mammal, but it lives on the sea-ice SURFACE and on land, and hunts from above the water rather than in it - treat it as an edge case in any 'ocean creature' list. Depth is a shallow DIVE range: typical dives 3-4.5 m, maximum recorded 13.9 m, most bears exceeding 6 m. Males reach about 2.5 m nose-to-tail, females 1.8-2 m. Notable for horizontal range rather than depth: tagged females have swum up to 687 km in 9 days.
polarbear.locationNote: Arctic sea ice over the continental shelf, plus shorelines when the ice retreats; hunts seals from the ice surface rather than underwater

lobster.fact: A record lobster taken off Nova Scotia in 1977 weighed 20.1 kg.
lobster.precision: Total body length (rostrum to tail fan); 1.06 m is the record individual, typical adults 20-60 cm. Depth: recorded intertidal to ~700 m depending on latitude, but most common at 4-50 m. Some sources cap the depth range at ~480 m.
lobster.locationNote: rocky and muddy bottoms off cold North Atlantic coasts, from tide pools out across the shelf

prawn.groupNote: 'Prawn' covers many caridean and penaeid shrimp; referent here is the northern prawn / northern shrimp, Pandalus borealis.
prawn.groupTaxon: 'Prawn' covers many caridean and penaeid shrimp; referent here is the northern prawn / northern shrimp, Pandalus borealis.
prawn.groupReferent: the northern prawn / northern shrimp, Pandalus borealis
prawn.fact: Starts life as a male, then switches to female partway through.
prawn.precision: Total length; 16.5 cm is a large female, males reach ~12 cm, typical animals much smaller. Usual depth 20-1330 m; extremes recorded 9-1450 m. Sex-change age varies with temperature (~2.5 yrs in warm areas, ~5 yrs in the Barents Sea). No IUCN assessment found.
prawn.locationNote: soft muddy bottoms of cold northern shelves and slopes; rises into the water column at night to feed

hermitcrab.groupNote: 'Hermit crab' names the superfamily Paguroidea (~1100 species); referent here is the common hermit crab, Pagurus bernhardus.
hermitcrab.groupTaxon: 'Hermit crab' names the superfamily Paguroidea (~1100 species); referent here is the common hermit crab, Pagurus bernhardus.
hermitcrab.groupReferent: the common hermit crab, Pagurus bernhardus
hermitcrab.fact: Lives inside an empty sea-snail shell and moves house as it grows.
hermitcrab.precision: Carapace length up to ~3.5 cm; whole-body length also quoted as ~35 mm, so the two figures are close but reported inconsistently. Depth from upper-shore pools to ~140 m. No IUCN assessment found.
hermitcrab.locationNote: rock pools and sandy or rocky seabed on North Atlantic coasts; small ones on the shore, big ones deeper

nudibranch.groupNote: 'Nudibranch' names the order Nudibranchia (~3000 species); referent here is the Spanish dancer, Hexabranchus sanguineus.
nudibranch.groupTaxon: 'Nudibranch' names the order Nudibranchia (~3000 species); referent here is the Spanish dancer, Hexabranchus sanguineus.
nudibranch.fact: Swims by flapping its mantle like a flamenco skirt - the Spanish dancer.
nudibranch.precision: Body length; 60 cm is the quoted maximum, commonly 25 cm, with ~40 cm animals reported from the Red Sea. Depth 1-50 m, usually 10-20 m. Crawls on the reef but genuinely swims when disturbed. No IUCN assessment found.
nudibranch.locationNote: sheltered Indo-Pacific coral and rocky reefs, over rubble and sand where sponges grow

sponge.groupNote: 'Sponge' names the phylum Porifera (~9000 species); referent here is the giant barrel sponge, Xestospongia muta.
sponge.groupTaxon: 'Sponge' names the phylum Porifera (~9000 species); referent here is the giant barrel sponge, Xestospongia muta.
sponge.groupReferent: the giant barrel sponge, Xestospongia muta
sponge.fact: Called the redwood of the reef; the big ones are over a century old.
sponge.precision: Height of the barrel; individuals exceed 2 m tall and 1.8 m across (3 m diameter reported). Age: the largest Conch Reef individuals were dated to ~130 years; a widely repeated 2300-year estimate is for one photographed, now-dead sponge and is disputed. No IUCN assessment found.
sponge.locationNote: hard-bottom reefs of the Caribbean, Bahamas, Bermuda, Florida and the Gulf of Mexico

clam.groupNote: 'Clam' is an informal term for many burrowing bivalves; referent here is the ocean quahog, Arctica islandica.
clam.groupTaxon: 'Clam' is an informal term for many burrowing bivalves; referent here is the ocean quahog, Arctica islandica.
clam.fact: One dredged off Iceland was 507 years old - the oldest animal ever aged.
clam.precision: Shell length; maximum ~13 cm. SeaLifeBase gives a benthic depth range of 0-482 m, but the species is concentrated far shallower (roughly 8-80 m in the US fishery). The 507-year individual ('Ming') was aged by shell growth increments after an initial 405-year estimate was revised upward. No IUCN assessment found.
clam.locationNote: burrowed into sand and mud on cool North Atlantic shelves, commonly 8-80 m off the US east coast

oyster.groupNote: 'Oyster' spans several bivalve families; referent here is the eastern (American) oyster, Crassostrea virginica.
oyster.groupTaxon: 'Oyster' spans several bivalve families; referent here is the eastern (American) oyster, Crassostrea virginica.
oyster.fact: One adult can filter up to about 190 litres of water in a day.
oyster.precision: Longest shell axis (usually reported as shell height for oysters). 20 cm is the commonly cited maximum (Texas Parks & Wildlife); SeaLifeBase/FishBase list a 35.5 cm record, MarLIN 18 cm; typical adults 15-25 cm. Depth: intertidal to roughly 10-11 m. The 50 US gal (190 L) per day filtration figure is a near-maximum laboratory rate; real reefs filter less.
oyster.locationNote: brackish estuaries and bars from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, forming reefs bared at low tide

mussel.groupNote: 'Mussel' covers the family Mytilidae (plus unrelated freshwater mussels); referent here is the blue mussel, Mytilus edulis.
mussel.groupTaxon: 'Mussel' covers the family Mytilidae (plus unrelated freshwater mussels); referent here is the blue mussel, Mytilus edulis.
mussel.fact: Anchors to rock with byssal threads - a glue that sets underwater.
mussel.precision: Shell length; usually 5-10 cm, exceptional individuals 15-20 cm, and some populations never exceed 2-3 cm. Depth: intertidal to ~40 m but overwhelmingly in the top few metres. No IUCN assessment found.
mussel.locationNote: dense beds on wave-washed rocks, piers and estuary shores of the cool North Atlantic

scallop.groupNote: 'Scallop' names the family Pectinidae; referent here is the Atlantic sea scallop, Placopecten magellanicus.
scallop.groupTaxon: 'Scallop' names the family Pectinidae; referent here is the Atlantic sea scallop, Placopecten magellanicus.
scallop.groupReferent: the Atlantic sea scallop, Placopecten magellanicus
scallop.fact: Has about 200 eyes that focus light with mirrors instead of lenses.
scallop.precision: Shell height (hinge to margin); maxima to 20 cm documented, typical adults ~8 cm and large ones ~17 cm. Depth usually 18-110 m, as shallow as 2 m in Maine and Canadian embayments and recorded to 384 m. Eye count varies with size - larger scallops carry more. No IUCN assessment found.
scallop.locationNote: sand and gravel beds of the northwest Atlantic shelf, from the Gulf of Maine to Georges Bank

barnacle.groupNote: 'Barnacle' names the infraclass Cirripedia; referent here is the northern acorn / common rock barnacle, Semibalanus balanoides.
barnacle.groupTaxon: 'Barnacle' names the infraclass Cirripedia; referent here is the northern acorn / common rock barnacle, Semibalanus balanoides.
barnacle.groupReferent: the northern acorn / common rock barnacle, Semibalanus balanoides
barnacle.fact: Cemented head-down to the rock, it kicks food in with its feathery legs.
barnacle.precision: Basal shell diameter, up to ~15 mm. This species is essentially exclusively intertidal (mean high to mean low water); the 10 m figure covers rare shallow-subtidal occurrences and is approximate. No IUCN assessment found.
barnacle.locationNote: bare rock, pilings and mussel shells on cool North Atlantic shores, densest in the mid-shore band

cockle.groupNote: 'Cockle' names the family Cardiidae; referent here is the common (edible) cockle, Cerastoderma edule.
cockle.groupTaxon: 'Cockle' names the family Cardiidae; referent here is the common (edible) cockle, Cerastoderma edule.
cockle.fact: Burrows only a few centimetres down and filters the tide passing above.
cockle.precision: Shell length; usually 3.5-5 cm, occasionally 6 cm. Predominantly intertidal; the 10 m lower limit (shallow sublittoral) is approximate. No IUCN assessment found.
cockle.locationNote: sandy and muddy tidal flats and estuaries of northwest Europe, exposed at every low tide

seacucumber.groupNote: 'Sea cucumber' names the class Holothuroidea (~1700 species); referent here is the giant California sea cucumber, Apostichopus californicus.
seacucumber.groupTaxon: 'Sea cucumber' names the class Holothuroidea (~1700 species); referent here is the giant California sea cucumber, Apostichopus californicus.
seacucumber.groupReferent: the giant California sea cucumber, Apostichopus californicus
seacucumber.fact: Breaks down its own guts each autumn and regrows them in spring.
seacucumber.precision: Relaxed body length; 50 cm commonly quoted, up to 60 cm reported (sea cucumbers stretch and contract, so lengths are soft numbers). Depth: low intertidal to 250 m. The autumn organ breakdown is seasonal atrophy plus regrowth, distinct from the defensive evisceration other holothurians perform. No IUCN assessment found.
seacucumber.locationNote: cobble, boulder and bedrock bottoms with moderate current, Gulf of Alaska to Baja California

seapen.groupNote: 'Sea pen' names the order Pennatulacea (~200 species); referent here is the orange sea pen, Ptilosarcus gurneyi.
seapen.groupTaxon: 'Sea pen' names the order Pennatulacea (~200 species); referent here is the orange sea pen, Ptilosarcus gurneyi.
seapen.groupReferent: the orange sea pen, Ptilosarcus gurneyi
seapen.fact: Not one animal but a colony of polyps, planted in mud by a muscular foot.
seapen.precision: Height of the erect colony above the seabed, to ~46 cm. Depth 14-225 m. Bioluminescence is well documented for this species but is display-only, triggered by disturbance rather than continuous. No IUCN assessment found. — species-G researched this animal independently (Ptilosarcus gurneyi, 14-225 m, height to 0.5 m, blue-green light): "Colour varies by genus: Ptilosarcus is reported as greenish-blue, while the Atlantic and Mediterranean Pennatula phosphorea flashes distinctly green. The travelling luminous wave is conducted by the colony’s nerve net."
seapen.locationNote: soft sand and mud bottoms on the Pacific coast of North America, Alaska to southern California
seapen.bioNote: Green-blue waves run up and down the stalk when touched, startling predators.

tubeworm.groupNote: 'Tube worm' is informal and covers many polychaete families; referent here is the giant hydrothermal vent tube worm, Riftia pachyptila.
tubeworm.groupTaxon: 'Tube worm' is informal and covers many polychaete families; referent here is the giant hydrothermal vent tube worm, Riftia pachyptila.
tubeworm.groupReferent: the giant hydrothermal vent tube worm, Riftia pachyptila
tubeworm.fact: It has no mouth and no gut; bacteria inside its body make all its food.
tubeworm.precision: Length of the chitin tube; adults commonly exceed 1 m, with reports to 2.4 m and occasional claims to 3 m. Depth is approximate - collections are documented at 2300-2600 m on the East Pacific Rise, with vent fields spanning roughly 2000 m (Guaymas Basin) to over 3000 m. Zone tagged 'abyssal' as the nearest fit; strictly these are mid-ocean-ridge vents, not abyssal plain. No IUCN assessment found.
tubeworm.locationNote: clustered on deep hydrothermal vents of the East Pacific Rise and Galapagos Rift, not the open plain

horseshoecrab.groupNote: 'Horseshoe crab' names the four living xiphosuran species; referent here is the Atlantic/American horseshoe crab, Limulus polyphemus.
horseshoecrab.groupTaxon: 'Horseshoe crab' names the four living xiphosuran species; referent here is the Atlantic/American horseshoe crab, Limulus polyphemus.
horseshoecrab.groupReferent: the Atlantic/American horseshoe crab, Limulus polyphemus
horseshoecrab.fact: Its blue blood is used worldwide to test medicines for bacterial toxins.
horseshoecrab.precision: Total length including the telson (tail spine); females to ~60 cm, males smaller, and regional averages are far less (Florida females ~21.5 cm). Depth mostly 1-11 m, recorded to ~61 m. IUCN Vulnerable (Smith et al. 2016 assessment).
horseshoecrab.locationNote: soft coastal bottoms from Maine to the Yucatan; crawls onto sandy beaches to spawn on spring tides

abalone.groupNote: 'Abalone' names the genus Haliotis (~50 species); referent here is the red abalone, Haliotis rufescens.
abalone.groupTaxon: 'Abalone' names the genus Haliotis (~50 species); referent here is the red abalone, Haliotis rufescens.
abalone.fact: The world's largest abalone; its shell is lined with rainbow nacre.
abalone.precision: Shell length to 31 cm, the largest of any abalone. Depth intertidal to over 180 m but most common at 6-40 m. IUCN Critically Endangered under the first global Haliotis assessment (2021, published 2022/2024).
abalone.locationNote: rocky reefs and kelp forests from British Columbia to Baja California, clamped to bare rock

limpet.groupNote: 'Limpet' is a shell shape shared by many unrelated gastropods; referent here is the common limpet, Patella vulgata.
limpet.groupTaxon: 'Limpet' is a shell shape shared by many unrelated gastropods; referent here is the common limpet, Patella vulgata.
limpet.fact: Its teeth are the strongest natural material known, up to 4.9 GPa.
limpet.precision: Shell length, to ~6 cm, typically 3-4 cm. Essentially an intertidal species from high shore to the sublittoral fringe; the 5 m lower bound is approximate. Tooth tensile strength 3.0-6.5 GPa (mean ~4.9 GPa) from goethite fibres in chitin (Barber et al. 2015).
limpet.locationNote: bare rock on wave-beaten northeast Atlantic shores, from the splash zone to the tide's lower edge

chiton.groupNote: 'Chiton' names the class Polyplacophora (~940 species); referent here is the gumboot / giant Pacific chiton, Cryptochiton stelleri.
chiton.groupTaxon: 'Chiton' names the class Polyplacophora (~940 species); referent here is the gumboot / giant Pacific chiton, Cryptochiton stelleri.
chiton.groupReferent: the gumboot / giant Pacific chiton, Cryptochiton stelleri
chiton.fact: The largest chiton on earth; its eight shell plates are buried in skin.
chiton.precision: Body length to 36 cm, over 2 kg. Depth is disputed: most sources say low intertidal to ~20 m, some to 60 m, and SeaLifeBase lists 600 m which looks unreliable. 20 m used as the defensible figure. No IUCN assessment found.
chiton.locationNote: low rocky shores and shallow reefs of the cold North Pacific, Japan to central California

seasquirt.groupNote: 'Sea squirt' names the class Ascidiacea (~3000 species); referent here is the vase tunicate / sea vase, Ciona intestinalis.
seasquirt.groupTaxon: 'Sea squirt' names the class Ascidiacea (~3000 species); referent here is the vase tunicate / sea vase, Ciona intestinalis.
seasquirt.groupReferent: the vase tunicate / sea vase, Ciona intestinalis
seasquirt.fact: Its tadpole larva has a notochord - the same rod our backbone grew from.
seasquirt.precision: Body length up to 15 cm (some sources say 12 cm). Depth from the lower shore to at least 500 m, but it is overwhelmingly a shallow, fouling-community animal. Widely introduced outside its native North Atlantic range. No IUCN assessment found.
seasquirt.locationNote: stuck to rock, weed, pilings and boat hulls in sheltered harbours and estuaries worldwide

parrotfish.groupNote: Parrotfishes, family Scaridae (~100 species, genera incl. Scarus, Sparisoma, Bolbometopon)
parrotfish.groupTaxon: Parrotfishes, family Scaridae (~100 species, genera incl. Scarus, Sparisoma, Bolbometopon)
parrotfish.measureNote: the largest species, the green humphead parrotfish Bolbometopon muricatum; most parrotfish are ~30 cm
parrotfish.fact: A big parrotfish can grind out hundreds of kilos of white reef sand a year.
parrotfish.precision: Family-level record. Size and depth are for the largest species, the green humphead parrotfish Bolbometopon muricatum (to 1.3 m, 0-40 m); most parrotfish are ~30 cm and live above 30 m. IUCN left null because the family has no single status - B. muricatum itself is Vulnerable. Sediment output is size-dependent and ranges from <3 to >5000 kg per fish per year across studies.
parrotfish.locationNote: coral reefs and reef flats in warm shallow coastal water

triggerfish.measureNote: the largest species, the titan triggerfish Balistoides viridescens; most triggerfish are smaller
triggerfish.fact: It locks into a reef crevice with a dorsal spine that a second spine bolts upright.
triggerfish.precision: Family-level record. Size and depth are for the titan triggerfish Balistoides viridescens, the largest species (75 cm TL, 0-60 m). Most triggerfish are smaller. IUCN null - no family-wide status.
triggerfish.locationNote: lagoons and seaward coral reef slopes in the tropics

bluetang.fact: Carries a switchblade spine at the tail base, flicked out to slash at attackers.
bluetang.precision: 31 cm TL from FishBase; usual depth 10-40 m. The name 'blue tang' is also used for the Atlantic Acanthurus coeruleus, a different species (2-50 m, ~39 cm).

remora.fact: Its suction disc is a dorsal fin rebuilt into slats; it rides sharks, turtles and ships.
remora.precision: Figures are for the live sharksucker, the most abundant and largest remora; the family Echeneidae has 8 species, several smaller.
remora.locationNote: warm seas, usually attached to a larger animal, sometimes free-swimming inshore

sailfish.fact: Long called the fastest fish, though recent work caps it nearer 35-55 km/h.
sailfish.precision: 3.48 m is fork length (FL); common length ~2.7 m TL. Depth 0-200 m with a report to 500 m off Brazil. IUCN Vulnerable (A2bd, assessed 2021, published 2022) - some secondary sources still say Least Concern. FishBase splits Atlantic (I. albicans) and Indo-Pacific sailfish; IUCN treats one cosmopolitan species. The old 110 km/h figure is not supported by direct measurement.
sailfish.locationNote: warm open ocean near the surface, often above the thermocline

mahimahi.fact: One of the fastest-growing fish: over a metre in year one, and dead by about five.
mahimahi.precision: 2.1 m TL max; usual depth 5-10 m. Maximum reported age ~5 years.
mahimahi.locationNote: warm open ocean surface waters, gathering under weed lines and floating debris

anchovy.groupNote: 'Anchovy' names the family Engraulidae (~150 species); figures here are the Peruvian anchoveta, Engraulis ringens
anchovy.groupTaxon: 'Anchovy' names the family Engraulidae (~150 species); figures here are the Peruvian anchoveta, Engraulis ringens
anchovy.fact: The Peruvian anchoveta is the largest single-species fishery on Earth.
anchovy.precision: 20 cm SL (standard length); a few sources give 24 cm. Catches ran 4.2-8.3 million tonnes/year over 2008-2012. IUCN assessed Least Concern in 2020.
anchovy.locationNote: cold upwelling water over the shelf off Peru and Chile

butterflyfish.measureNote: the largest species, the lined butterflyfish Chaetodon lineolatus; most are 7–25 cm
butterflyfish.fact: Many butterflyfish pair for life and patrol one stretch of reef together for years.
butterflyfish.precision: Family-level. ~129 species in ~12 genera; most are 7-25 cm, largest (lined butterflyfish Chaetodon lineolatus) 30 cm TL. 200 m is an approximate family envelope - individual species ranges are much narrower (C. melannotus 2-20 m; C. lineolatus 2-171 m). IUCN null - no family status.
butterflyfish.locationNote: coral reefs, from shallow lagoons down to dim mesophotic reef

damselfish.groupNote: Damselfishes, family Pomacentridae (~385 species, includes the anemonefishes)
damselfish.groupTaxon: Damselfishes, family Pomacentridae (~385 species, includes the anemonefishes)
damselfish.measureNote: the largest species, Microspathodon dorsalis; the smallest, Chrysiptera giti, is 4.5 cm
damselfish.fact: Damselfish farm algae gardens and chase off fish and divers many times their size.
damselfish.precision: Family-level. ~385 species; smallest Chrysiptera giti 4.5 cm, largest Microspathodon dorsalis 45 cm. Shallow coastal waters to ~200 m, but only Chromis is recorded below 80 m. IUCN null - no family status. Anemonefish/clownfish are also Pomacentridae.
damselfish.locationNote: coral and rocky reefs, hovering just above a defended patch of bottom

goby.groupNote: Gobies, family Gobiidae (>2,000 species in >200 genera)
goby.groupTaxon: Gobies, family Gobiidae (>2,000 species in >200 genera)
goby.measureNote: the tank goby Glossogobius giuris; most gobies are under 10 cm
goby.fact: Gobies are the largest family of marine fish - more than 2,000 species.
goby.precision: Family-level. depthMaxM left null - no reliable family-wide maximum; most gobies live in shallow water. Max length 50 cm SL is the tank goby Glossogobius giuris; most gobies are under 10 cm, and the family includes some of the smallest vertebrates known (Trimmatom nanus, ~8-10 mm). Habitat given as marine, but Gobiidae also includes brackish and freshwater species.
goby.locationNote: perched on sand, rubble and reef in shallow coastal water and tide pools

blenny.measureNote: the largest of ~400 species; most blennies are under 10 cm
blenny.fact: Blennies wedge into empty shells and holes and watch the world from the doorway.
blenny.precision: Family-level. ~400 species in ~58 genera; most under 10 cm, largest ~54 cm. Most are intertidal/shallow, a few descend to about 450 m. IUCN null - no family status.
blenny.locationNote: rocky shores, tide pools and shallow reef, in crevices and empty shells

opah.fact: The only fish known to keep its whole body warmer than the water around it.
opah.precision: 2 m TL, up to ~270 kg. Usually found between 50 and 400 m. The genus Lampris was split into several species in 2018, so older records under L. guttatus may include other species.
opah.locationNote: open ocean, cruising the cold twilight water below the sunlit layer

wahoo.fact: A 113 cm wahoo has been timed at about 77 km/h - among the fastest of all fish.
wahoo.precision: 250 cm TL from FishBase. Depth is disputed: FishBase gives 0-20 m (usually 0-12 m) while other compilations report to ~183 m. Speed figures for large fish (>100 km/h) are extrapolations, not measurements.
wahoo.locationNote: warm open ocean, often alone above deep water near drop-offs and wrecks

cobia.fact: The only member of its family, it shadows sharks and rays the way a remora does.
cobia.precision: 2 m TL. FishBase gives an extreme depth range of 0-1200 m; in practice cobia are a shelf and inshore fish found in the upper tens of metres, so the 1200 m figure should be treated as an outlier record.
cobia.locationNote: warm shelf seas, around buoys, wrecks, reefs and large swimming animals

lanternfish.measureNote: Lampanyctus crocodilus; most lanternfish are 2–15 cm
lanternfish.fact: Lanternfish make up as much as 65% of all deep-sea fish biomass.
lanternfish.precision: Family-level: ~246-250 species in ~33 genera. Max length 30 cm is Lampanyctus crocodilus; most lanternfish are 2-15 cm. Global biomass estimates of 550-660 million tonnes are widely quoted but highly uncertain - the ICES paper puts mesopelagic fish biomass anywhere from ~1,000 to ~20,000 million tonnes. The 65% share of deep-sea fish biomass is a commonly cited estimate, not a precise measurement. Day/night depths are family generalisations; not every species migrates and ranges differ by species and region.
lanternfish.locationNote: open ocean worldwide; they are the deep scattering layer sonar sees as a false seabed
lanternfish.bioNote: Belly photophores erase its silhouette; tail lights signal to mates.
lanternfish.diel: Rises to the surface layer at night to feed and sinks back to the twilight zone by day - the largest animal migration on Earth.

bristlemouth.groupNote: Bristlemouths, genus Cyclothone (13 species, family Gonostomatidae)
bristlemouth.groupTaxon: Bristlemouths, genus Cyclothone (13 species, family Gonostomatidae)
bristlemouth.measureNote: Cyclothone atraria; most Cyclothone are 2–8 cm
bristlemouth.fact: Cyclothone may number in the quadrillions - the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.
bristlemouth.precision: Genus-level: 13 living species. Depth and max length are from Cyclothone atraria (298-4938 m, usually 400-2400 m; 6.2 cm SL); most Cyclothone are 2-8 cm. The quadrillion estimate is extrapolated from fine-mesh net catches and is order-of-magnitude only. Bristlemouths, largely Cyclothone, are reported to make up over 50% of all vertebrate individuals between 100 and 1000 m. Unlike lanternfish, Cyclothone largely does not perform daily vertical migration.
bristlemouth.locationNote: open ocean twilight and midnight zones, most often around 1,000 m down
bristlemouth.bioNote: Rows of belly photophores match the dim light from above and hide its outline.

copepod.fact: Copepods likely outnumber every other multicellular animal group on Earth.
copepod.precision: Subclass-level. Typical adults 1-2 mm; free-living species range from ~0.2 mm to 17 mm (parasitic forms are larger). depthMaxM null - copepods occur at all ocean depths and no single maximum is meaningful; Calanus glacialis alone spans 0-1800 m. Copepods make up 55-95% of metazoan zooplankton in the open ocean. Bioluminescence is real but confined to a minority of marine genera (e.g. Metridia, Pleuromamma, Oncaea); most copepods do not glow. Habitat marked marine, though many copepods are freshwater.
copepod.locationNote: everywhere in the water column, from coastal shallows to the deep open ocean
copepod.bioNote: Some species squirt glowing clouds from skin glands to dazzle a predator.
copepod.diel: Many species rise to feed near the surface at night and sink hundreds of metres by day.

amphipod.fact: Amphipods swarm every deep-sea carcass; nearly 11,000 species are described.
amphipod.precision: Order-level: 10,966 described species. Max length 34 cm is the supergiant Alicella gigantea (recorded 3,890-8,931 m); the vast majority of amphipods are a few millimetres to ~2 cm. 11,000 m depth is from Hirondellea gigas in hadal trenches (~6,800-11,000 m). Most amphipods are benthic, but some (e.g. Themisto, hyperiids) are fully planktonic. Habitat marked marine, though amphipods also occur in fresh water and on land.
amphipod.locationNote: on and just above the seabed everywhere, from beach sand to the deepest trenches

arrowworm.fact: Second only to copepods in the plankton - and a voracious predator of them.
arrowworm.precision: Phylum-level: ~100-130 species. Size range 2-120 mm; most are 1-2 cm, so 12 cm is the extreme. Biomass is commonly put at 10-30% that of copepods. Depth 4000 m reflects specialised bathypelagic species; a few chaetognaths go deeper still. Bioluminescence set false for the group, but at least one deep-sea species (Caecosagitta macrocephala) does produce light.
arrowworm.locationNote: drifting in the water column worldwide, densest in the sunlit surface layer

foraminifera.groupNote: Foraminifera - shelled single-celled protists (thousands of living species)
foraminifera.groupTaxon: Foraminifera - shelled single-celled protists (thousands of living species)
foraminifera.fact: These single cells build about 25% of all the calcium carbonate in the ocean.
foraminifera.precision: Not an animal - a group of shelled single-celled protists, included as an abundance champion. Typical test diameter 0.1-1 mm; a few large benthic species exceed 1 cm. depthMaxM null - forams occur at all depths, but calcareous tests dissolve below roughly 4,000 m. Their tests form Globigerina ooze covering ~130 million km2 of seafloor. Planktonic foraminifera supply ~32-80% of deep-sea carbonate. benthic set true because most species live in sediment, but planktonic forams live in the water column.
foraminifera.locationNote: in and on seafloor sediment everywhere, plus drifting species in the open water

fireflysquid.fact: Spawning swarms turn Toyama Bay's shoreline electric blue each spring.
fireflysquid.precision: Size is usually cited as ~7.5 cm total body length; some sources instead report 7-8 cm mantle length, so the measure is given as overall length. Everyday depth is 200-400 m, with records to ~1200 m. Not assessed by IUCN.
fireflysquid.locationNote: deep water of the northwest Pacific and Sea of Japan; crowds into Toyama Bay to spawn in spring
fireflysquid.bioNote: thousands of photophores on belly, arm tips and eyes; blue counterillumination

dragonfish.fact: Females reach 40 cm; males stay about 5 cm, with no gut and no teeth.
dragonfish.precision: Popular sources credit this fish with red bioluminescence, but the confirmed far-red (>700 nm) suborbital producers are the loosejaw dragonfishes Malacosteus, Aristostomias and Pachystomias (Herring & Cope 2005); red emission in Idiacanthus is not established in the primary literature, so bioColour is given as blue-green. FishBase lists 1239-2000 m; females migrate above 500 m at night while males stay deep. Not assessed by IUCN.
dragonfish.locationNote: open-ocean midwater of the southern subtropics and temperate south, roughly 25 to 60 degrees south
dragonfish.bioNote: rows of belly photophores plus a glowing barbel lure below the chin

viperfish.fact: Its fangs are so long they close outside the jaw, past the eyes.
viperfish.precision: FishBase gives 200-4700 m, usually 494-1000 m. Maximum length 35 cm. Lure function of the elongated first dorsal ray is inferred from anatomy and captive observation rather than filmed in the wild.
viperfish.locationNote: open-ocean midwater worldwide; rises toward the surface at night with the scattering layer
viperfish.bioNote: belly photophores hide its shape; a lit dorsal ray dangles as a lure

hatchetfish.groupNote: marine hatchetfishes, family Sternoptychidae - Argyropelecus, Sternoptyx and Polyipnus
hatchetfish.groupTaxon: marine hatchetfishes, family Sternoptychidae - Argyropelecus, Sternoptyx and Polyipnus
hatchetfish.measureNote: Argyropelecus gigas; the family runs down to ~2.8 cm (Polyipnus danae)
hatchetfish.fact: A blade-thin silver body and tubular eyes locked upward to spot silhouettes.
hatchetfish.precision: Group record. Sizes across the family run from Polyipnus danae at ~2.8 cm to Argyropelecus gigas at ~12 cm, the figure used here. Depth is the family envelope; individual species migrate within it (A. aculeatus 300-600 m by day, 100-300 m at night). Conservation status not assessed at family level.
hatchetfish.locationNote: open-ocean twilight zone worldwide, mostly a few hundred metres down by day
hatchetfish.bioNote: downward-pointing belly photophores dimmed to match the light from above

atolla.fact: When seized it spins a pinwheel of blue flashes to call in a bigger predator.
atolla.precision: Bell is usually 2-10 cm across; 15 cm is the maximum on SeaLifeBase. The 'burglar alarm' interpretation comes from Edith Widder's work and underlies the e-Jelly lure. Not assessed by IUCN. Measure is bell diameter, not an armspan or disc width in the ray sense.
atolla.locationNote: deep open-ocean midwater worldwide, in the permanently dark midnight zone
atolla.bioNote: burglar-alarm pinwheel of blue light around the bell rim, fired when attacked

flashlightfish.fact: Schools of them blink over coral reefs on moonless nights.
flashlightfish.precision: The light is NOT made by the fish: it comes from symbiotic luminous bacteria (Candidatus Photodesmus katoptron) housed in the subocular organ, which glow continuously while the fish shutters them by rotating the organ downward. FishBase gives 35.0 cm TL and 2-400 m. Not assessed by IUCN.
flashlightfish.locationNote: coral reef caves and drop-offs of the tropical west Pacific; out over open water on dark nights
