flashlightfish.bioNote: a bean-shaped organ under each eye, rolled down to blink; light is bacterial

cookiecutter.fact: Bites round plugs of flesh from tuna, whales and even submarine sonar domes.
cookiecutter.precision: Maximum 42 cm for males, 56 cm for females. Depth usually 0-1000 m with records to ~3700 m. Ventral photophores are described as emitting a greenish glow that persists up to about three hours after death; the non-luminous collar acting as a decoy silhouette is the standard interpretation but has not been tested experimentally.
cookiecutter.locationNote: open ocean worldwide in warm water; deep by day, near the surface at night
cookiecutter.bioNote: glowing green belly erases its shadow; a dark collar mimics a small fish

crystaljelly.fact: Its glow gave science GFP, the green marker protein behind a Nobel Prize.
crystaljelly.precision: The primary emission is blue (~470 nm) from the calcium-activated photoprotein aequorin; green fluorescent protein re-emits it as green, so the observed colour is green. No reliable maximum depth is published - the species is epipelagic and nearshore, so depthMaxM is left null rather than guessed. Bell 10-25 cm. Not assessed by IUCN.
crystaljelly.locationNote: nearshore surface water of the northeast Pacific, from the Bering Sea to central California
crystaljelly.bioNote: aequorin fires blue at the bell rim; GFP shifts it to green

seasparkle.fact: A single cell up to 2 mm wide, big enough to see without a microscope.
seasparkle.precision: Cell diameter 0.4-2 mm, typically ~0.5 mm; measure is cell diameter, not a body length. It regulates buoyancy with internal ammonium and sits at or near the surface, so no meaningful maximum depth is published. Populations along the US west coast have lost the ability to luminesce (Valiadi et al. 2019). Not assessed by IUCN.
seasparkle.locationNote: coastal surface water worldwide; blooms light the surf at night and stain the sea pink by day
seasparkle.bioNote: flashes blue for under 0.1 s when jostled by waves, boats or swimmers

dinoflagellate.groupNote: bioluminescent bloom-forming dinoflagellates, chiefly Lingulodinium polyedra, Pyrodinium bahamense and Noctiluca scintillans
dinoflagellate.groupTaxon: bioluminescent bloom-forming dinoflagellates, chiefly Lingulodinium polyedra, Pyrodinium bahamense and Noctiluca scintillans
dinoflagellate.fact: Every breaking wave sets off the flash; it is a startle response, not a glow.
dinoflagellate.precision: Group record for a phenomenon rather than one organism, so size and depth are left null: individual cells are tens of micrometres to ~2 mm across, and a bloom has no length. Light comes from a luciferin-luciferase reaction triggered by mechanical shear. Not all dinoflagellates are luminous and not every red tide glows.
dinoflagellate.locationNote: warm sheltered bays and surf zones; brightest in Mosquito Bay, Vieques, and off southern California
dinoflagellate.bioNote: each cell flashes blue when sheared, so waves and wakes light up

siphonophore.groupNote: order Siphonophorae, colonial hydrozoans - Praya, Apolemia, Erenna, Physalia
siphonophore.groupTaxon: order Siphonophorae, colonial hydrozoans - Praya, Apolemia, Erenna, Physalia
siphonophore.fact: A colony, not one animal: each body part is a separate specialised zooid.
siphonophore.precision: Group record. maxLenM is the ~47 m outer ring of the Apolemia filmed off Ningaloo in 2020 by Schmidt Ocean Institute; the total colony was estimated at over 100 m but not measured, and Praya dubia is separately recorded at 40-50 m. No firm published depth ceiling for the order, so depthMaxM is null; the red-lured Erenna was filmed at 1600-2300 m. Almost all siphonophores luminesce but the function is largely unstudied. Erenna's red lure was the first red bioluminescence found in any marine invertebrate.
siphonophore.locationNote: open-ocean water column at every depth; the giant ones drift in deep submarine canyons
siphonophore.bioNote: most flash blue; deep Erenna twitches glowing red lures to draw fish in

pyrosome.fact: A hollow tube of thousands of clones, all filtering water and jetting it out one end.
pyrosome.precision: Light is widely attributed to symbiotic luminous bacteria (Photobacterium) in paired light organs beside each zooid's siphon, but a 2020 transcriptome study found a candidate pyrosome luciferase homologous to Renilla luciferase, so the mechanism is genuinely unsettled. Colony length to ~60 cm for this species; the related Pyrostremma spinosum reaches many metres. Diel migration typically 0-750 m with records to ~2500 m. Not assessed by IUCN.
pyrosome.locationNote: warm and temperate open ocean and shelf water; rises to the surface at night, sinks by day
pyrosome.bioNote: the whole tube pulses blue-green; one colony's flash sets off its neighbours

glasssquid.groupNote: family Cranchiidae, ~60 species of glass or cockatoo squids - Galiteuthis, Teuthowenia, Bathothauma
glasssquid.groupTaxon: family Cranchiidae, ~60 species of glass or cockatoo squids - Galiteuthis, Teuthowenia, Bathothauma
glasssquid.fact: Transparent except for its eyes and gut, which it hides behind mirrors and light.
glasssquid.precision: Group record; maxLenM left null deliberately because the family spans ~10 cm mantle length in typical glass squids to over 3 m in the colossal squid Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni, and a single number would misrepresent either end. Depth is approximate: cranchiids occur from the surface to below 2 km. Not all species have been checked for photophores. Not assessed by IUCN at family level.
glasssquid.locationNote: open-ocean twilight and midnight water column in every ocean
glasssquid.bioNote: photophores under each eye cancel the one shadow a see-through body still casts

barreleye.fact: Its green tubular eyes swivel inside a clear, fluid-filled dome on its head.
barreleye.precision: This species is not known to produce light itself - it is a watcher of other animals' light, hanging motionless and looking up for silhouettes. Other barreleyes do luminesce: Opisthoproctus soleatus carries symbiotic Photobacterium phosphoreum in a rectal bulb and projects the light downward through a reflective ventral 'sole'. Usually seen at 600-800 m, with the wider range given here. Not assessed by IUCN.

gulpereel.fact: Its jaw is a loose net bigger than the rest of its body.
gulpereel.precision: Tail-tip organ is described as glowing pink with occasional red flashes; the emission spectrum has not been measured, so 'red' is the reported appearance rather than a quantified wavelength - unlike the loosejaw dragonfishes, where far-red emission is instrumented. Length usually given as 80 cm, with some sources reporting up to 1 m.

gulpereel.bioNote: a light organ on the whip-tail tip glows pink with occasional red flashes

tripodfish.fact: Perches on stiffened fin rays and faces the current, waiting for food to drift by.
tripodfish.precision: No bioluminescence is documented for this species; it is nearly blind and hunts by touch with its raised pectoral fin rays. Commonly over 30 cm standard length, to 43.4 cm total length. IUCN Least Concern, assessed 2013.
tripodfish.locationNote: soft sediment of the abyssal plain and lower slope in tropical and temperate oceans

lanternshark.fact: Luminous markings beside its dorsal spines may warn predators off.
lanternshark.precision: The light is intrinsic, NOT bacterial - Duchatelet et al. (2019) showed no bacterial luminescence, and emission is hormonally controlled by melatonin and prolactin. Depth 70-2490 m, usually 200-500 m. Benthopelagic: it swims close to the bottom rather than resting on it, so benthic is false. IUCN Vulnerable on the 2021 global assessment (population reduction 30-49%); earlier and regional assessments differ (Near Threatened in the northeast Atlantic, Least Concern in the Mediterranean).
lanternshark.locationNote: continental slope of the eastern Atlantic, Norway to Gabon, and the Mediterranean
lanternshark.bioNote: thousands of belly photophores glow blue-green (486 nm) to cancel its silhouette

zones.name: Epipelagic zone
facts: The only layer with enough light for photosynthesis.
Holds the vast majority of commercial fisheries.
zones.precision: NOAA calls the upper 200 m the euphotic or sunlight zone. The base is conventionally the depth where photosynthetically active radiation falls to 1% of surface value, which is 200-250 m in the clearest ocean water and far shallower in turbid coastal water.

zones.name: Mesopelagic zone
facts: Too dark for photosynthesis, lit mainly by bioluminescence.
Source of the daily vertical migration, Earth's largest animal migration.
zones.precision: 200-1000 m is the standard definition (NOAA, WHOI). WHOI notes recent acoustic estimates put twilight-zone fish biomass around 10 billion tonnes, possibly ten times earlier estimates - that figure is contested and is not used as a headline fact.

zones.name: Bathypelagic zone
facts: No sunlight at all reaches this layer.
Pressure runs from roughly 100 to 400 atmospheres.
zones.precision: Pressure figure follows the standard 1 atm per 10 m of depth. WHOI describes the midnight zone as the single largest habitat on Earth, often quoted as about 70% of all seawater; that share depends on where you set the boundaries, so it is left out of the headline facts.

zones.name: Abyssopelagic zone
facts: Named from the Greek for bottomless.
Water sits near freezing, around 2-3 degrees Celsius.
zones.precision: 4000-6000 m is the standard definition. Below about 4000 m calcium carbonate shells dissolve, leaving a seafloor of brown clay and silica.

temperature.label: Surface
temperature.note: Global average sea surface temperature is about 17 C; the observed range across the world ocean surface is about -2 to 36 C.
temperature.precision: Global mean, not a local reading.

temperature.label: Base of the mixed layer
temperature.note: The wind-mixed surface layer is roughly isothermal to 100-200 m, so 200 m is still near surface temperature; the main thermocline begins here and falls steeply below.
temperature.precision: Set to null deliberately. No source found gives a global mean temperature at exactly 200 m; Britannica describes the thermocline as running from about 200 m to about 1000 m with temperature falling from roughly 20 C at the top to about 2 C at the bottom, but that 20 C is a low-latitude figure and would be badly wrong at high latitudes.

temperature.label: Base of the thermocline
temperature.note: Below the thermocline the ocean is nearly isothermal; sources put this depth at about 2-4 C.
temperature.precision: Sources disagree: Britannica gives about 2 C below the thermocline, while the bathypelagic zone (1000-4000 m) is commonly described as a near-constant 4 C. Point value left null and the disagreement expressed as a range.

temperature.label: Abyssal
temperature.note: Abyssal water sits at about 2-3 C through the great majority of its volume; the global average of 2000 m water is about 2.5 C.
temperature.precision: Point value left null; 2-3 C is the sourced band. For context, the average temperature of all ocean water from surface to seafloor is about 3.5 C.

lightRemaining.note: Only 16% of surface light is still present at 10 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Clear open-ocean water. For reference the same source gives 45% remaining at 1 m, because infrared is absorbed almost immediately.

lightRemaining.note: About 1% of the original light is left at 100 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Clear open-ocean water. The 1% level is the conventional base of the euphotic zone, which is why the euphotic depth can be as shallow as 100 m in some water and 200-250 m in the very clearest.

lightRemaining.note: Under 1% remains; NOAA states there is rarely any significant light beyond 200 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Set to null deliberately. No source found gives a numeric percentage at exactly 200 m. 200 m is the conventional 1%-of-surface euphotic depth in the clearest water, so the true value is at or below 1% and is often far lower.

lightRemaining.note: Effectively zero; 1000 m is the deepest sunlight reaches under the best conditions.
lightRemaining.precision: Set to null deliberately. NOAA: sunlight may travel about 1,000 m into the ocean under the right conditions, but there is rarely any significant light beyond 200 m. Below 1000 m is the aphotic zone, where no sunlight penetrates.
